guidance: Type the purity as it is stamped: 585 is 14 karat, 750 is 18 karat and 925 is sterling silver. Karat exists only for gold. The figure is a declared purity, not an assay — only X-ray fluorescence or a laboratory assay can tell a genuine stamp from a false one — and the page gives no value or price for the metal.
method: Karat is a mass fraction in parts per 24, so a karat value becomes millesimal fineness by multiplying by 1000/24: 14 karat is 583.33 parts per thousand and 18 karat is exactly 750. A percentage becomes parts per thousand by multiplying by 10, and parts per thousand is the unit the calculation works in. Because a hallmark is rounded to three figures, the value is then matched to the nearest published mark for its metal: gold 999 (24 karat), 916 (22), 750 (18), 585 (14), 500 (12), 417 (10), 375 (9) and 333 (8); silver 999 fine, 958 Britannia, 925 sterling, 900 coin, 835 and 800; platinum 999.5, 999, 950, 900, 850 and 750. This is why 14 karat, at 583.3 parts per thousand, carries a 585 stamp, and the difference from the matched mark is reported alongside it; 585 read as karat is 14.04. Karat is only defined for gold, so a karat input with silver or platinum is refused instead of being converted. An optional piece mass splits into fine metal M x fineness / 1000 and the alloy balance M - fine metal, both rounded to a milligram. Inputs are limited to 0.1 to 1,000 parts per thousand, 0.1 to 100 percent, above 0 to 24 karat and a piece mass of 0 to 100,000 grams. Warnings appear at exactly 1,000 parts per thousand, which is pure metal on paper rather than a stamp, and below the lowest common mark for the metal. The page converts a declared purity: it does not assay the piece, infer a mark from density, value the metal or account for stones, solder or plating.

sources.title: Fineness — karat as parts per 24 by mass, millesimal fineness as parts per 1,000, and the standard gold, silver and platinum marks, including 585 for 14 karat, 916 for 22 karat and 925 for sterling
